topic: Corked thigh: what helps in the first few days

slides.headline: Corked thigh: go gentle early on
slides.sub: What tends to help in the days after a knock to the thigh.

slides.title: What a cork actually is
slides.body: A corked thigh is a deep bruise in the thigh muscle, usually from a knee or hard knock in contact sport. Bleeding in the muscle causes pain, swelling and stiffness.

slides.title: First 48 hours: calm it down
slides.body: Relative rest, ice for about 15 to 20 minutes every couple of hours, compression and elevation are common early steps. Resting with the knee gently bent can help too.

slides.title: Skip the HARM early on
slides.body: In the first couple of days, avoid heat, alcohol, running and massage on the area. These can increase bleeding in the muscle and may slow early recovery.

slides.title: Get moving gradually
slides.body: As pain allows, gentle knee bending, walking and light cycling help restore movement. Build towards jogging and sport in steps rather than testing it with a flat-out sprint.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Swelling or pain that keeps increasing, a thigh that feels very tight or numb, being unable to bend the knee, or a lump that stays hard deserves prompt medical assessment.

caption:
Copped a knee to the thigh at touch footy or cricket? Here's what tends to help in the first few days.

A corked thigh is a deep bruise in the muscle, and early care makes a real difference. In the first 48 hours, relative rest, ice, compression and elevation are common steps. Skip the HARM: heat, alcohol, running and massage on the area can increase bleeding in the muscle.

As pain allows, gentle knee bending, walking and light cycling help restore movement, then build towards jogging and sport in steps. Swelling or pain that keeps increasing, a thigh that feels very tight or numb, or being unable to bend the knee needs prompt medical assessment.
